question_text: A 43-year-old woman visits her primary care provider complaining of fatigue. Although she has had it for several months, her fatigue has been worsening over the past few weeks. She has no other symptoms. Past medical history is significant for hypertension. She takes chlorthalidone, an oral contraceptive pill, and a multivitamin every day. Family history is noncontributory. She drinks about 1 bottle of wine every day and started taking a shot or two of whisky or vodka every morning before work to “clear out the cobwebs”. She was recently fired from her job. Today, her heart rate is 90/min, respiratory rate is 17/min, blood pressure is 110/65 mm Hg, and temperature is 36.7°C (98.1°F). On physical exam, she appears malnourished and anxious. Her conjunctiva are pale, and glossitis is noted on oral exam. Her heart has a regular rate and rhythm and her lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. She has no gait or balance abnormalities. Lab results show a hemoglobin of 10 g/dL, with a mean corpuscular volume (MCV) of 108 fl. Elevated level of which of the following will most likely to be found in this patient?

### Enhanced Information Summary:

The patient presents with symptoms and lab findings indicative of macrocytic anemia, characterized by a high mean corpuscular volume (MCV) and low hemoglobin. Macrocytic anemia is commonly caused by deficiencies in Vitamin B12 or folate. The presence of pale conjunctiva and glossitis further supports the likelihood of a nutritional deficiency, potentially exacerbated by her high alcohol consumption, which can impair nutrient absorption and lead to deficiencies.

Vitamin B12 deficiency specifically leads to elevated levels of methylmalonic acid (MMA) and homocysteine. MMA is a more specific marker for Vitamin B12 deficiency as it accumulates when Vitamin B12 is deficient, affecting the conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA. Elevated homocysteine can also result from Vitamin B12 deficiency but is less specific as it can also be elevated in folate deficiency.

The retrieved evidence paths support the association between macrocytic anemia and nutritional deficiencies, particularly pointing towards interactions involving Vitamin B12. These paths confirm the role of Vitamin B12 in the pathogenesis of macrocytic anemia and its deficiency leading to elevated MMA, aligning with the medical consensus.

Given the patient's symptoms, lab results, and lifestyle factors, the most likely elevated marker in this patient would be methylmalonic acid, directly linked to Vitamin B12 deficiency. Homocysteine could also be elevated but is less specific to Vitamin B12 deficiency alone.
